channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You cannot stop yourself from imagining an impossible scenario.
item.description: Counterfactual thinking is your brain's persistent attempt to simulate 'what if' scenarios to understand outcomes.

item.title: You judge people by their actions, but yourself by intent.
item.description: Research suggests the actor-observer asymmetry is highly context-dependent rather than a universal cognitive bias.

item.title: New memories actively overwrite what you already remembered.
item.description: Retroactive interference describes the inhibition or competitive interference that makes it difficult to retrieve older memories due to the acquisition of new, similar information.

item.title: You cannot find the word you know you know.
item.description: The tip-of-the-tongue state represents a partial retrieval failure where you access the definition but not the label.

item.title: Your focus on a weapon blinds you to everything else.
item.description: When a weapon is present during a crime, witnesses remember fewer details about the perpetrator and the scene.

item.title: Your brain blocks out memories to clear the way.
item.description: Proactive interference occurs when your older memories disrupt your ability to recall newer information.

item.title: You claim to know things that do not exist.
item.description: When presented with lists containing fictional concepts, many people claim they are familiar with them.

item.title: Speaking two languages physically reorganizes your brain's efficiency.
item.description: Some studies suggest that bilingual individuals may demonstrate an advantage in specific executive function tasks, though this remains a subject of intense scientific debate and is not considered a universally established fact.

item.title: You value information simply because a successful person said it.
item.description: Prestige bias is the tendency to assign greater weight to the opinions of people who are high-status, regardless of their expertise in the specific topic.

item.title: The faster your city, the less likely you are to help.
item.description: A 1999 study of 31 cities found a correlation between an aggregate 'pace of life' index—which included walking speed, work speed, and public clock accuracy—and the likelihood to assist a stranger.

item.title: You believe every category has a hidden, unchanging truth.
item.description: Psychological essentialism explains your tendency to assume that groups—like gender or race—possess an immutable, internal 'essence'.

item.title: You fail to reach goals by ignoring obstacles ahead.
item.description: Mental contrasting demonstrates that visualizing success without anticipating specific obstacles actually reduces your goal-directed energy.

item.title: You remember the punchline far better than the context.
item.description: Research indicates that information presented in a humorous way is often recalled better than neutral information, though this effect is moderated by the relevance of the humor to the content.

item.title: You overestimate your personal consistency.
item.description: The 'end of history illusion' suggests that people consistently fail to anticipate how their personality and preferences will shift over time.

item.title: You don't know what you want until you see it.
item.description: Preference construction theory demonstrates that people do not have fixed internal values; instead, they build their preferences in the moment of choice.

item.title: You value things more when they are scarce.
item.description: Research shows that participants in a 1975 study rated identical items as significantly more valuable simply because they were told supply was limited.

item.title: You underestimate how much control you have over your habits.
item.description: Research indicates that people who view willpower as a limited resource perform worse on self-control tasks than those who don't.

item.title: You are more creative when the font is harder to read.
item.description: Cognitive disfluency—the experience of difficulty in processing information—can trigger more deliberate, analytic thinking.

item.title: You see yourself as less capable than you are.
item.description: When tasks are difficult, people consistently exhibit a worse-than-average effect, underestimating their relative performance.

item.title: Your brain ignores most of the visual world.
item.description: Change blindness results suggest that visual perception is not a continuous, high-definition recording, highlighting the dependency of visual awareness on focused attention.

item.title: You value things more just because you made them.
item.description: The IKEA effect demonstrates that people assign higher value to projects or products when they have personally contributed to their creation.

item.title: You fear losing more than you value gaining.
item.description: Prospect theory suggests that the psychological pain of losing $100 is roughly twice as intense as the pleasure of gaining $100.

item.title: You prioritize fairness only when it benefits you.
item.description: In the ultimatum game, participants often reject 'unfair' offers, even when rejecting means they lose all potential money themselves.

item.title: Your physical environment dictates how you judge social interactions.
item.description: A 2008 study by Williams and Bargh reported that participants holding a warm drink rated a target person as having a 'warmer' personality, but this finding has been disputed by later attempts to replicate the effect.

item.title: You ignore the most common outcome because it feels boring.
item.description: The conjunction fallacy occurs when you judge a specific scenario as more probable than a general one, despite mathematical laws.

item.title: Your desire for closure changes the way you process information.
item.description: A 1993 study found that individuals with a higher desire for closure form opinions faster and are more resistant to changing them when presented with new evidence.

item.title: You only notice your stress when you stop moving.
item.description: The incubation effect, as described by Graham Wallas in his 1926 book 'The Art of Thought,' suggests that creative solutions often emerge after you stop consciously focusing on a problem.

item.title: You perform worse when you feel forced into a task.
item.description: Research into learned helplessness shows that repeated exposure to uncontrollable situations leads to subsequent passive behavior, even when control is regained.

item.title: You are already preparing your next words while speaking.
item.description: A 1986 study showed that speech errors occur because we process phonemes for future words before finishing current ones.

item.title: Recalling a memory makes it vulnerable to being altered.
item.description: Research indicates that when a memory is reactivated, it enters a plastic state where it can be modified before being re-stored.

item.title: Your memory for stories morphs to fit your culture.
item.description: A 1932 study found that over multiple retellings, recalled stories became shorter, simpler, and more aligned with existing cultural schemas.

item.title: You create memories of things that never actually happened.
item.description: The study found that about 50% of participants reported being sure they heard the lure word.

item.title: Remembering a single detail can cause you to forget others.
item.description: A 1994 study demonstrated that repeatedly recalling a subset of learned information suppresses memory for related, unrecalled items.

item.title: You forget what others say when you are waiting.
item.description: In a 1982 study, participants showed significantly lower recall for information delivered immediately before their own turn to speak.

item.title: Writing down your preferences makes you choose the wrong thing.
item.description: A 1993 study showed that participants who listed reasons for their preferences were less satisfied with their choices than those who chose intuitively.

item.title: You are a more accurate judge when you feel sad.
item.description: In a 2009 study, participants in a negative mood were significantly less susceptible to the misinformation effect than those in a positive mood.

item.title: Your eyes do not see, they perform a search.
item.description: Yarbus's 1967 study showed that saccadic gaze patterns are task-dependent, providing foundational empirical data that supports the theory that vision is an active process of fixations rather than a passive, continuous feed.

item.title: The smell of citrus makes you act more cleanly.
item.description: A 2005 study found that people who were exposed to a lemon scent kept their environment significantly cleaner.

item.title: You trust information more if it is presented clearly.
item.description: A 1999 study by Reber and Schwarz showed that cognitive fluency influences truth judgments.

item.title: Silence in a conversation creates a false sense of rejection.
item.description: Wesselmann et al. (2011) found that silence used as an act of social exclusion (being ignored) is perceived as ostracism.

item.title: People who feel warm coffee view strangers as friendlier.
item.description: A 2008 study by Williams and Bargh suggested that holding a hot beverage increases the perception of a stranger's warmth, but subsequent attempts to replicate these findings have failed.

item.title: You overestimate how clearly others see your inner emotions.
item.description: In a 1998 study, people consistently predicted their anxiety would be obvious to observers, even when it remained invisible.

item.title: You judge risk based on how a question is phrased.
item.description: A 1974 study found that describing a car accident as 'smashing' instead of 'hitting' led people to estimate higher speeds.

item.title: Your decision-making changes when you are distracted by numbers.
item.description: In a 1999 study by Shiv and Fedorikhin, participants holding a 7-digit number (high cognitive load) chose chocolate cake 63% of the time, compared to 41% for those holding a 2-digit number.

item.title: You struggle to change your mind even when presented with new facts.
item.description: A 2015 study found that repeated exposure to false claims makes them seem true, even when they contradict existing knowledge.

item.title: You misremember your past self to fit your current values.
item.description: A 1986 study by Ross and Conway demonstrated that individuals recall their past attitudes as more similar to their current ones than they actually were.

item.title: You act as if you are being watched even when alone.
item.description: A 2006 study showed that people are significantly more honest in tasks when a picture of eyes is displayed nearby.

item.title: You rate a choice as better after you have already made it.
item.description: A 1956 study demonstrated that participants immediately increased their preference for a chosen item and decreased it for a rejected one.

item.title: You spend more time on tasks that offer no reward.
item.description: A 2006 study by Kivetz, Urminsky, and Zheng found that people persist with a task longer if they believe they are making progress, even if the progress is fake (the 'illusionary progress effect').

item.title: You forget the length of a painful experience entirely.
item.description: In a 1996 study, patients expressed a higher willingness to return for a repeat procedure if the duration was extended but the end was less painful.
